rebase.title: Rebasing gives commits new identities
rebase.intro: Rebase the same topic twice: once while it is private, and once after a teammate has built on it.
rebase.scope: An owned training repository. Commit IDs are shortened and illustrative. Replaying a commit onto a new parent creates a new commit object with a new ID; the old commit stays reachable from the reflog until it is cleaned up. Hosting rules for force-pushes are separate.

sources.title: Git reference: git-rebase, including Recovering from upstream rebase

steps.title: Inspect the history
steps.explanation: Your topic commit T1 has parent B. main has since gained M1. Nobody else has fetched the topic, so you own its history.

steps.title: Replay onto main
steps.explanation: git rebase main reapplies T1’s change after M1. The new commit T1′ has a different parent, so it has a new ID. The old T1 is no longer on the branch; the reflog keeps it as a recovery point.

steps.explanation: git log --graph --oneline --all shows main as an ancestor of the topic. The new parent context needs fresh tests and review before you publish it.

steps.explanation: T1 was pushed and a teammate pulled it, then committed T2 on top. Their branch now refers to T1’s ID.

steps.title: Rewrite and force-push
steps.explanation: You rebase onto main and force-push. The remote topic now points to T1′. --force-with-lease would stop you overwriting work you had not fetched, but it is not permission to rewrite history others use.

steps.title: The teammate merges
steps.explanation: Their next pull merges T1′ into a branch that still contains T1. History now holds the same change twice under two IDs, and reviews of T1 no longer match the branch.

steps.title: Coordinate instead
steps.explanation: Agree before rewriting shared work. The teammate then rebases T2 onto the new topic; Git skips the change T1′ already contains, leaving one copy of it.
